title: US and Iran Sign Peace Deal at Versailles, Ending Three Months of Strait of Hormuz Closure
summary: On 17 June, President Trump and Iranian President Pezeshkian signed a memorandum of understanding at the G7 summit in Versailles to end the conflict that began in late February 2026. The deal includes a commitment to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20% of the world's seaborne crude oil and LNG passes — lifting what the International Energy Agency described as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market. The deeper question now is how quickly, and how fully, global energy flows can recover.
context:
- The conflict began on 28 February 2026 when the United States and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran targeting its nuclear and ballistic missile infrastructure. Iran retaliated by declaring the Strait of Hormuz 'closed' on 4 March, deploying drones, ballistic missiles, and fast attack boats against vessels attempting to transit the 34-kilometre-wide waterway.

- The Strait is the world's most critical oil chokepoint. Before the conflict, roughly 20% of global crude oil and 20% of global LNG flowed through it daily. There is no alternative pipeline route capable of absorbing that volume at short notice — making closure uniquely disruptive to energy markets worldwide.

- The economic consequences were immediate and severe. Tanker traffic fell to near zero within days. By April, the IMO reported approximately 2,000 ships and 20,000 seafarers stranded in the Persian Gulf. The energy shock fed directly into the May 2026 US CPI reading of 4.2% — a three-year high — with energy prices up 23.5% year-on-year.

- The deal is interim rather than permanent. Under the agreement, Iran will facilitate safe passage for commercial vessels for 60 days while a broader settlement is negotiated. Goldman Sachs estimates Gulf oil flows may recover to only 70% of pre-war levels over the medium term, reflecting the time required for insurance markets, shipping routes, and supply chains to normalise.

- The wider implication is for long-term energy security strategy. Three months of Hormuz closure compressed years of geopolitical risk modelling into a live stress test. Governments and energy importers are now expected to accelerate strategic reserve reviews, LNG contract diversification, and domestic energy transition investments in ways that will persist long after tanker flows resume.

title: Warsh's Fed Drops Forward Guidance and Signals Possible Rate Hike in Hawkish First Meeting
summary: The Federal Open Market Committee held rates unchanged at 3.50%–3.75% at its June meeting — the first under new Chair Kevin Warsh — but the broader signal was a sharp shift in institutional posture. The dot plot flipped from implying a rate cut this year to signalling a potential hike, and Warsh stripped the Fed's statement of forward guidance language for the first time in over a decade. This was not merely a rate decision; it was the opening statement of a new operating philosophy at the world's most influential central bank.
context:
- Warsh succeeded Jerome Powell on 22 May, appointed by President Trump after years of friction between the White House and the Powell Fed over the pace of rate cuts. Warsh served on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors from 2006 to 2011, earning a reputation as an inflation hawk and balance-sheet sceptic during the post-crisis era of quantitative easing.

- His central critique of the post-2008 Fed is its over-reliance on forward guidance — the practice of pre-announcing future rate paths to anchor market expectations. Warsh argues this constrains policy flexibility and creates complacency, and has cited Alan Greenspan's data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach as his preferred model.

- The practical consequence of abandoning forward guidance is greater rate uncertainty for markets. Under Powell, investors had grown accustomed to months of advance signalling before policy moves. Removing that mechanism raises the term premium embedded in long-duration bonds and increases cross-asset volatility — particularly when the economic outlook is already unclear.

- Warsh notably declined to submit his own interest rate projections in the dot plot, an unusual step that underscores his commitment to discretion over pre-commitment. Nine of his FOMC colleagues, however, now project at least one rate hike by year-end — a sharp reversal from March, when the median projection implied a cut.

- The backdrop makes Warsh's position unusually complex. The May CPI of 4.2% is driven principally by an energy shock from the Iran conflict — a supply-side problem that rate hikes cannot directly remedy. Yet the Fed's credibility rests on being seen to prioritise price stability regardless of inflation's source. Warsh's first meeting set the tone: vigilance, without a pre-announced playbook.

title: Trump Announces Apple-Intel Chip Partnership, Accelerating US Semiconductor Push
summary: President Trump announced on 18 June via Truth Social that Apple has agreed to work with Intel to design and manufacture chips in the United States — a move that, if completed, would mark the first time Apple has used a domestic foundry for production since ending its CPU relationship with Intel in 2020. The announcement reflects both the ambitions of US industrial policy and Apple's deepening strategic interest in reducing its near-total dependency on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC).
context:
- Apple has manufactured virtually all of its custom silicon — from iPhone A-series chips to M-series Mac processors — at TSMC's leading-edge fabs in Taiwan since 2016. TSMC controls an estimated 90% of the world's most advanced chip production, making Taiwan a single geographical point of failure for global consumer electronics and a growing share of the digital economy.

- The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 allocated $52 billion in US federal subsidies to rebuild domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. Intel was positioned as the primary vehicle for domestic foundry services under its Intel Foundry Services division, launched in 2021 as part of a broader strategic reinvention. An Apple partnership — even at the entry level — would provide the volume and commercial validation that Intel's foundry business has so far lacked.

- Geopolitical pressure over Taiwan has intensified corporate supply chain thinking across the technology sector. The 2026 Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure — while geographically separate — served as a live reminder of how swiftly a single chokepoint can disrupt global trade, reinforcing boardroom interest in geographic diversification of critical production.

- The deal, which neither Apple nor Intel confirmed in immediate public statements, is expected to begin with lower-end processors — likely chips for MacBooks or non-pro iPhone models — as early as 2027 or 2028. TSMC is expected to remain Apple's primary supplier for its most advanced processes for the foreseeable future, meaning Intel would initially serve as a complementary rather than replacement partner.

- Intel's road to becoming a credible foundry has been long and costly, marked by years of process delays and significant market share losses in PCs and data centres. A confirmed Apple contract would represent the most important commercial proof point for Intel's foundry ambitions — validating its recovery thesis for investors and potentially attracting further hyperscaler customers.
